titulo: The real actuator: latency, torque limit and actuator network
lead: Between the policy deciding and the motor turning there is a network, the controller loop and the motor PD. In this lesson you measure the "real robot" latency (delay) with a step on the knee, count the falls that 20 and 40 ms cause under a push, and compensate the kp identified in lesson 3.
objetivo: measure the actuator latency on the bench, count the falls it causes under a push, and compensate kp in the command.

aprende.t: The layers of time: policy at 50 Hz, network, PD at 500 Hz–1 kHz
Native latency in MuJoCo 3.5+: the actuator's delay attribute
Falls under a push with 0, 20, and 40 ms of latency
Compensate the identified kp and watch the "real" robot walk

hero_alt: A robot rotary actuator on a bench test with an inertia disc and a torque sensor, with a blurred oscilloscope in the background.

secoes.titulo: The path from command to torque

nos.detalhe: The G1 policy decides every 20 ms (the step_dt in deploy.yaml): it reads the state and returns 29 position targets.

Time between the state being read and the target reaching the motor: inference, network, controller queue. In MuJoCo 3.5+, the actuator stores the last commands (history) and applies the one from N ms ago.
On the robot, the PD runs in the motor driver, much faster than the policy: torque = kp × (target − q) − kd × velocity.
Each joint has a maximum torque (in the Menagerie MJCF, 139 N·m at the knee and 5 N·m at the wrist pitch and yaw). A command above that is clipped: the joint does not do what the policy asked.

secoes.legenda: Latency and saturation are invisible in a calm walk and show up under a push.

secoes.titulo: Three ways to model the actuator
secoes.sub: From the simplest to what you use when the simple one is not enough.

texto: What MuJoCo and Isaac Lab do without you asking: the torque comes out instantly, exactly equal to the PD. It is the "sim" from lesson 1.

Adds the measured latency and the declared torque limit. MuJoCo 3.5+ handles the latency by itself (delay and nsample on the actuator); the kit fills the history with the first command so it does not start from a zero target.
With sysid (lesson 3) and randomization around the measured value, this is what many projects do.
A small neural network learns, from real motor data, the relationship between command, position history, and delivered torque, and enters the simulator in place of the ideal PD.
Worth it when the actuator has effects that a single parameter does not capture. It requires a motor test bench; this course only mentions it.
NVIDIA's GR00T-WholeBodyControl stack added, on 08/31/2026, per-motor kp and kd scaling against stumbling in the SONIC policy: sim-to-real is also fine-tuning the PD at deploy time.
E3 in this lesson does the minimal version: it multiplies the commanded kp by the inverse of the identified one.

secoes.titulo: Measure the latency and count the falls
secoes.sub: --medir gives a 0.3 rad step at the knee with the robot hanging. --ms runs the walk with 6 pushes (120, 150, and 180 N for 0.2 s, forward and sideways) per latency.

blocos.rot: Terminal · measure the latency on the bench

abas.html:
degrau de 0,3 rad no joelho esquerdo, robô pendurado: tempo até o encoder mexer 0,005 rad
  sim:               8 ms
  real:             30 ms
atraso medido (real − sim): 22 ms

The "real" takes 22 ms longer than the sim to move the knee: the 20 ms of hidden latency plus a bit from the softer kp, which also slows the response.

atraso   quedas em 6 empurrões   (120/150/180 N, frente e lado, 0,2 s, t = 3 s)
   0 ms  2/6   . . . . x x
  20 ms  3/6   x x x . . .
  40 ms  6/6   x x x x x x
(x = caiu, . = ficou de pé; ordem: 120, 150, 180 N para a frente e depois para o lado)

At 40 ms, it falls in all six. At 0 ms, it still falls in two side pushes; at 20 ms, in the three front ones.

Don't conclude that "20 ms is better from the side than 0 ms." These are six trials with one seed: the fall pattern wobbles; what you read is the count rising with latency (2, 3, 6). To claim more, add more pushes and directions.

secoes.sub: Lesson 3 identified kp ≈ 0.57 of the commanded value. Sending 1/0.57 ≈ 1.75 times the kp, the "real" motor delivers close to what the policy expects.

abas.html:
política: unitree_rl_lab G1 29 GDL velocity v0 (ONNX, 480 entradas) · comando 0.50 m/s · 10 s
sim                          queda: não · andou 5.1 m em 10 s (vel. 0.51 m/s; pedida 0.50)
real simulado                queda: não · andou 4.5 m em 10 s (vel. 0.45 m/s; pedida 0.50)
saída: 0

The "simulated real" now walks 4.5 m and doesn't fall (exit 0). The sim, with the stiffer kp, keeps walking. The latency, the mass, and the friction are still there: the policy handles it, because the biggest difference was corrected.

exercicios.texto: Apply the step to the knee in both worlds.
Run the walk with pushes at 0, 20, and 40 ms.
Use the kp you identified in lesson 3 (1 divided by it) and run both worlds again.
exercicios.pronto: python3 kit/dois_mundos.py --kp-comando 1.75; echo "saída: $?" → real simulado … queda: não and saída: 0.

secoes.sub: The explanation appears after your answer.

perguntas.p: With no push, the policy walks with the "real" robot's 20 ms of latency (lesson 1). With a push, 40 ms knocks it down in 6 of 6. What does this teach?
opcoes: That latency only matters when the robot is standing still.
That the push is what measures the margin that latency takes away.
That the policy was trained with exactly 40 ms of fixed latency.
That MuJoCo ignores latency during normal walking.
perguntas.explica: In a calm walk, the policy corrects with room to spare. A push demands a fast reaction, and that's where every millisecond counts. A robustness test needs a disturbance.

perguntas.p: MuJoCo 3.5+ models latency in the actuator itself. What does the kit do in addition at startup?
opcoes: It fills the command history with the first target.
It turns off latency for the first 20 ms of simulation.
It raises kp to compensate for the latency.
It swaps the integrator so latency doesn't accumulate.
perguntas.explica: The history starts zeroed: without filling it, the first N ms send a zero target to the joints, a jolt that doesn't exist on the robot.

perguntas.p: When is it worth training an actuator network instead of PD with latency?
opcoes: Whenever the robot has more than 20 joints.
When the simulator has no position actuator.
When the actuator has effects that a few parameters can't capture.
When no measured data from the real motor is available yet.
perguntas.explica: The network learns the command → torque relationship from motor data. It needs that data; without it, PD with latency and sysid is the way.

itens.texto: A step on the knee with the robot hanging measures the latency: 22 ms.
Under a push, falls rise from 2/6 (0 ms) to 6/6 (40 ms).
Sending kp divided by the identified value makes the "simulated real" walk without falling.
